newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Korean decision on Fokker seen delayed.
newsitem.headline: Korean decision on Fokker seen delayed.

text.p: Administrators of the bankrupt Dutch planemaker Fokker NV said on Friday that they did not expect a decision on the future of Fokker from the South Korean government before the end of November.
South Korea's Samsung Aerospace Industries has been given exclusive access to Fokker's accounts with a view to a possible takeover of its core planemaking business.

Samsung on Wednesday said involvement of the South Korean government was not at issue, saying: "The only government approval Samsung needs is from the central bank of Korea on capital investment abroad."
"Administrators (for Fokker) anticipate no decision from the Korean government before the end of November," a statement from the administrators' office said.
"In the event of a positive decision the final negotiations and conclusion of final contracts of all the parties involved would continue for some more weeks," the statement said.
Recent Dutch media reports have suggested that a review of the rescue deal by the Seoul government might be delaying negotiations over Fokker.

A South Korean government spokesman earlier this week said that the government could not tell Samsung what to do about Fokker. "It's a private project paid for by a private company," said Yu Jeong-yeol of the aerospace industry industry division at the South Korean ministry of trade.
Court-appointed administrators have been running Fokker since it was declared bankrupt in March. Two months ago they gave Samsung exclusive rights to go through Fokker's books.
Earlier this month Dutch Economic Affairs Minister Hans Wijers said he expected a decision "within days" by Samsung.
Samsung, which sees Fokker as a way of breaking into the global aerospace industry, is unwilling to assume all the risks in the company and wants major investment by the Netherlands.
The Hague government has said it wold provide capital and invest in a new 125-seat regional jet, but Samsung is said to have baulked at demands for long-term Dutch job guarantees.
Earlier this week Samsung said it was looking for a partner to help rescue Fokker. De Volkskrant newspaper reported on Friday that Samsung was having no luck in its search.
Fokker has struggled in recent years to achieve financial stability and swapped industry partners several times.

In 1993, Daimler Benz Aerospace (DASA) paid 686 million guilders for a 51 percent stake in Fokker, but depressed world aircraft markets and a weak dollar saw the company sink into deep losses that had to be met by DASA and the Dutch state.
In January 1996, Daimler cut off all financial support, forcing the company into bankruptcy in March. -- Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
